title: Delay Hard Training Today
description: Sleep duration, HRV, and resting heart rate have all moved meaningfully against your personal baseline in the same night — the same three-signal pattern as a high recovery deficit, framed specifically around today's training decision. Recommends postponing HIIT/max-effort work and swapping in aerobic or mobility work instead.
source: Huberman Lab (training/recovery balance); evidence-informed trigger combination

conditional.question: Your sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate all look off from your baseline today — should today's hard training wait?
conditional.yesLabel: Yes, swap today's session for something easier
conditional.noLabel: No, I feel normal, keep today's plan

actions.frequency: Once, on the day this triggers
actions.details: Move any planned intervals, max lifts, or high-intensity conditioning to a later day when the three signals have recovered. Reassess against the next night's data before resuming full intensity.

actions.action: Swap in aerobic or mobility work
actions.frequency: Once, on the day this triggers
actions.details: Easy Zone 1/2 cardio, a walk, or a mobility/stretching session in place of the planned hard session, so the training habit continues without adding further sympathetic/cardiovascular load.

benefits: Avoids stacking hard training on top of a genuine, three-signal-confirmed recovery deficit
Reduces injury and illness risk associated with training through significant autonomic strain
Keeps the recommendation specifically actionable for today's training plan rather than general rest advice
science: Concurrent reductions in sleep duration and HRV alongside an elevated resting heart rate are well-established markers of unresolved autonomic/sympathetic strain. Training at high intensity while all three are depressed is associated with elevated injury and illness risk and blunted training adaptation, so postponing the hardest-effort work (rather than training volume broadly) is the targeted response for this specific decision.
contraindications: Not a reason to skip all training — the recommendation is to postpone the hardest-effort portion, not stop training entirely
If this state persists for multiple consecutive days, treat as a stronger signal to reduce training volume more broadly and consider consulting a coach or physician

evidence_metadata.scientific_rationale: Same three-signal pattern (sleep duration < 85% baseline, HRV < 85% baseline, resting HR > 105% baseline, 1 night) as the recovery-deficit 'high' tier in docs/oura-rules/recovery-deficit.json. Deliberately kept at identical thresholds rather than invented separately, since these are meant to represent the same underlying physiological state (high recovery deficit) viewed through a training-decision lens rather than a competing definition of it.

evidence_for_protocol.notes: Avoiding hard/high-intensity training during genuine multi-signal autonomic strain, in favor of easier aerobic or mobility work, is directly and repeatedly supported by Huberman Lab training-and-recovery content. This is the training-decision framing of the same recommendation already present as an action inside the recovery-deficit high tier ('reduce high-intensity training').

evidence_for_trigger.notes: Thresholds are copied intentionally from the recovery-deficit high tier's worked example rather than independently derived, so this rule is a companion/alternate framing of that same state, not a new validated threshold set.

expected_effect.short_term: Reduced same-day sympathetic/cardiovascular training load; HRV/RHR are not expected to normalize same-day.
expected_effect.long_term: Consistently deferring hard training during genuine 3-signal recovery deficits should reduce cumulative strain and lower overtraining/illness risk, though untested as a rule.
